result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.maximal_independent_set()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a maximal independent set in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L34993-L35123){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.maximal_independent_set( nodes=None, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Maximal independent set](/assets/graphs/maximal-independent-set.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph: a triangle 2, 3, 5 with pendant nodes 1 and 4. Nodes 2 and 4, in the accent color, share no edge, and every other node is adjacent to one of them, so no node can be added. The card shows the result [2, 4], size 2, smaller than the maximum of 3." width="100%"} A maximal independent set is an independent set that cannot be extended by adding any other vertex. In other words, every vertex not in the set is adjacent to at least one vertex in the set. "Maximal" is weaker than "maximum": the result cannot grow, but a different choice of nodes might yield a larger set. This uses a randomized greedy algorithm: it shuffles the candidate nodes, then walks through them, adding each node that is not adjacent to a node already chosen. Because the shuffle changes from run to run, different calls can return different (equally valid) sets unless `seed=` is fixed. Typical uses include: - picking a batch of mutually non-conflicting jobs, tasks, or resources - selecting well-spread "representative" nodes, since every other node is adjacent to one - generating many cheap candidate solutions (see `find_maximal_independent_sets()`) when hunting for a large independent set For the largest set the library can find, use `maximum_independent_set()`, which uses a deterministic degree-based heuristic. Edge direction is ignored, as in `is_independent_set()`: on a directed graph, an edge `A -> B` means `A` and `B` can't both be chosen. Self-loops are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional starting set of node IDs that must appear in the result. These nodes must already form an independent set; the algorithm keeps them and extends the set until it is maximal. If `None` (the default), the algorithm starts from an empty set. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed controlling the order in which candidate nodes are considered. Passing the same integer always gives the same result on the same graph, which is useful for reproducible analyses and tests. If `None` (the default), the order is drawn from system entropy, so repeated calls may return different sets. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs forming a maximal independent set, sorted in ascending order. An empty graph gives an empty list. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the starting nodes don't form an independent set (have adjacent nodes). [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If any starting node doesn't exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Randomized greedy fills a set by visiting the nodes in a random order, adding each node that is not yet excluded, and excluding its neighborhood from further consideration. This takes $O(V + E)$ time with $O(V)$ auxiliary memory, and the result is guaranteed *maximal* (no further node can be added) but not necessarily *maximum*, which is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard to compute exactly. Supplying `seed=` locks reproducibility; passing `nodes=` fixes a starting independent set that the algorithm then extends. For the largest possible set, `maximum_independent_set()` runs a different (still greedy but degree-aware) heuristic. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 5-node path `1-2-3-4-5`, a maximal independent set picks nodes that are never adjacent. Depending on the order, it has 2 nodes (like `2` and `4`) or 3 nodes (`1`, `3`, and `5`). Showing the labels makes the chosen nodes easy to check: ::: {#1eed0683 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(5) mis = graph.maximal_independent_set(seed=23) [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in mis] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['2', '4'] ``` ::: ::: Different seeds can give different sets, all of them valid and maximal: ::: {#896c8c0b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} results = [graph.maximal_independent_set(seed=s) for s in range(5)] [(len(r), graph.is_independent_set(r)) for r in results] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [(3, True), (2, True), (2, True), (2, True), (2, True)] ``` ::: ::: Passing a starting node forces the algorithm to build its set around it, which is useful when you already know one node must be included: ::: {#e8fa0dc6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(6) first_node = graph.get_node_ids()[0] mis = graph.maximal_independent_set(nodes=[first_node], seed=23) # Returns True: the requested starting node is always included first_node in mis ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: This scheduling-style example treats conflicting jobs as connected nodes, so a maximal independent set identifies a batch of jobs that can all run at the same time: ::: {#f70be78a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["Job_A", "Job_B", "Job_C", "Job_D"]) .add_edges( [ ("Job_A", "Job_B"), # A conflicts with B ("Job_B", "Job_C"), # B conflicts with C ("Job_C", "Job_D"), # C conflicts with D ] ) ) parallel_jobs = graph.maximal_independent_set(seed=23) # Returns the labels of jobs that can run simultaneously [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in parallel_jobs] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['Job_A', 'Job_C'] ``` ::: :::
